the media's role in constructing explanations for the vote was a major factor contributing to the conventional wisdom of the 1984 election, but not the only one.

(1) the 1984 election was interpreted by the media as a referendum on Reagan's performance, (2) the media interpreted this as a positive referendum, (3) the media attributed this positive interpretation to the economy, and (4) the media attributed the positive economic interpretation to the Reagan economic program.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the media, in this case, did not provide an accurate account of the public's preferences.
the media and the public are both more interested in the process of the election than in the outcome, and more interested in the candidates than in the issues.
the media's coverage of elections and politics is a process of social construction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
election explanations are constructed in a process that is neither purely rational nor purely irrational; rather, it is a process of social interaction that combines elements of both.
the process of constructing explanations is a powerful force shaping the political environment.

the process of constructing explanations for election outcomes has implications for public policy, and that the constructed explanation for an election is likely to be more influential in the policy-making process than the "real" reason that voters made the choice they did.
